message:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.
response:
Here's everything in order, starting with the bag, since that's the one with a real catch.

## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

It depends on the airline, and on several common ones it won't. At 56 × 36 × 23 cm and 9 kg, your bag is borderline. These were the typical limits at my last update; airlines change them, so check yours:

| Airline | Cabin bag limit | Your bag (56 × 36 × 23 cm, 9 kg) |
|---|---|---|
| TAP Air Portugal | 55 × 40 × 20 cm, 8 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 3 cm too deep, 1 kg over |
| Ryanair (Priority) | 55 × 40 × 20 cm, 10 kg | ✗ too long and too deep |
| Lufthansa | 55 × 40 × 23 cm, 8 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 1 kg over |
| KLM | 55 × 35 × 25 cm, 12 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 1 cm too wide |
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 23 kg | ✓ |
| easyJet (large cabin bag, paid) | 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 15 kg | ✓ |

The 23 cm depth is the usual problem, since many airlines cap it at 20 cm. A strict gate agent will make you check it, which is exactly what you want to avoid. If you tell me your airline, I can give you a straight yes or no.

**Plan for gate-checking anyway.** Wheeled bags often get sent to the hold at the gate on full flights, even when they fit. Keep everything you can't lose in your personal item: laptop, chargers, medication, and one change of clothes.

## Three things to do on a free evening

Next week is late November, so sunset is around 5:15–5:20 pm and showers are likely. Bring a light waterproof and shoes with grip. Lisbon's limestone pavements are hilly and slippery when wet.

1. **A miradouro (viewpoint), then a walk through Alfama.** Senhora do Monte and Graça have the widest views. Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol sit right above Alfama's lanes, so you can walk straight down into them afterwards. If work keeps you past sunset, the city lights are still worth it.
2. **Fado.** This is Lisbon's traditional music: melancholic, intimate, and best heard in a small room. Alfama and Mouraria have dinner-with-fado houses, which usually need booking. In Bairro Alto there are informal *tascas* where amateurs sing (*fado vadio*). Check recent reviews, because venues change.
3. **Eat and drink your way around.** Time Out Market (Mercado da Ribeira) is easy for a solo diner, with lots of stalls under one roof. Then head to Bairro Alto's street bars or the calmer Príncipe Real. Try a *ginjinha*, a cherry liqueur, and a *pastel de nata*.

Tram 28 is famous, but it's packed and a known pickpocket spot. Keep your phone and wallet in front pockets.

## Saying "thank you"

It depends on **who is speaking**, not who you're thanking:

- **Obrigado** (oh-bree-GAH-doo) if you're a man
- **Obrigada** (oh-bree-GAH-dah) if you're a woman
- **Muito obrigado/a** means "thank you very much"

In everyday Lisbon speech the first syllable is often swallowed, so you'll hear something closer to "brigad-oo". Locals won't mind either way, and the effort is appreciated.

## Tipping

Tipping isn't expected the way it is in the US, but it is appreciated:

- **Cafés and casual places:** round up or leave small change.
- **Sit-down restaurants:** 5–10% for good service is generous. Service is rarely included on the bill.
- **Cash is easier,** because card machines often have no tip option.

One local habit to know is the **couvert**. Bread, olives, butter or cheese placed on the table on arrival are charged if you eat them. Politely send them back if you don't want them.

## Rolling or folding work shirts

**Fold shirts; roll everything else.**

- **Shirts:** button them, fold them around a piece of card or a magazine (or use a packing folder), and lay them flat on top. Rolling creases collars and fronts.
- **Casual items:** roll t-shirts, knitwear, underwear and gym clothes, and use them to fill the gaps.
- **On arrival:** hang shirts in the bathroom while you shower, and the steam drops most creases. Most business hotels can also lend you an iron.
- **Non-iron shirts** make a three-day trip much easier.

Wear your bulkiest items, such as your jacket and heavier shoes, on the plane. That also keeps weight off the bag's 9 kg.

## Out-of-office message

> Thank you for your message. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date] and will have limited access to email. I'll reply as soon as I can after I'm back on [date].
>
> If your request is urgent, please contact [Name] at [email / phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

To keep it warm but professional:

- **Don't name the destination.** Many people prefer not to publicise when they're away.
- **Do name a real backup contact.** Clients value that more than anything else in the message.

## Luggage tag colour

Pick something unusual: **fluorescent orange, lime green or hot pink**. Black, navy and red are on half the bags at the carousel. A bright ribbon or strap on the handle helps too.

After losing your case in the spring, a **Bluetooth tracker** (AirTag, Tile or similar) inside the bag is worth adding. It's fine in the cabin and invaluable if the bag gets gate-checked. Put your phone number and email on the tag, but not your home address.

## Making the Friday return easier

- **Pack on Thursday night.** Leave out only Friday's clothes and toiletries.
- **Check out in the morning.** Either leave your bag with the hotel or take it to your meetings if the venue has space. Not having to go back to the hotel saves a lot of time.
- **Check in online and download your boarding pass** before the meetings start.
- **Allow plenty of time.** Lisbon airport is close to the centre, about 20–30 minutes by taxi, Uber or Bolt, but it's often crowded, and Friday evening traffic is heavy. Aim to arrive about 2 hours before departure. Allow more if you're leaving the Schengen area, as UK flights do, because of passport control. The EU's newer biometric entry/exit checks can add time for non-EU passport holders.
- **Check your terminal.** Terminal 2 is used mainly by low-cost airlines and isn't on the metro. You reach it by a free shuttle bus from Terminal 1, so add 10–15 minutes.
- **Book your ride** during your last meeting break rather than at the kerb.
- **Keep your liquids bag at the top** of your carry-on, and change into something comfortable before you head to the airport.

Have a great trip.
